<x_0.2588><y_0.1656>_War-Horse._ The proper rules for choofing a horfe
for fervice in war, are thefe: he should be tall in flat-
ture, with a comely head, and out-fwelling forehead.
His eye thould be bright and fparkling, and the white
part of it covered by the eye brow. The cars thould
be final, thin, short, and pricking; or if long, they
thoul be moveable with cafe, and well carried. The
neck thould be deep, and the breast large and fwelling.
The ribs bending, the chine broad and fraight, and
the buttocks round and full. The tail thould be high
and broad, neither too thick nor too thin; the thigh
fwelling; the leg broad and flat, and the pattern flont.
When fuch a horfe is chofen, he muft be kept high du-
ring the time of his teaching, that he may be full of
vigour. His food muft be fweet hay, and good clean oats,
or two parts of oats and one part of beans or peafe,
well dried and hardened. The quantity thould be half
a peck in the morning, and the fame quantity at noon
and in the evening Upon his refling days he is to be
drefled between five and fix in the morning, and water-
ed at fever or eight. In the evening he is to be drefled
at four, and watered about five, and he muit always
have provender given him after watering; he muft be
littered about eight, and then muft have food gi-
ven him for all night. The night before he is ridden
all his hay is to be taken away about nine o'clock, and
he muft have a handful or two of oats about four in
the morning: when he has eaten thefe, he is to be
turned upon the fnaffle, and rubbed very well with dry
cloths; then faddled, and made fit for his exercise.
When he has performed this, he is to be brought
fweating into the flable, and rubbed down with dry
wifps. When this has been done, the faddle is to be
taken off, and he is to be rubbed down with dry cloths;
the houfing cloth is then to be laid on; and the faddle
being again laid on, he is to be walked gently about
till thoroughly cool. After this, he muft ftand with-
out meat two or three hours, then he muft be fed; and
in the afternoon he is to be rubbed and drefled as be-
fore, and watered in the ufual manner.<x_0.9912><y_0.7273><class_Text>

<x_0.2725><y_0.7227>_Horse Worm_, in natural history, a species of fly-
worm called alfo _bott_, produced of eggs deposited by a
two-winged fly of the shape and fize of the humble
bee in the intestines of horses. See BOTTS.<x_0.9922><y_0.7828><class_Text>

<x_0.3086><y_0.7797>_Ricur-Horse_, in zoology. See HIPPOPTAMUS.<x_0.96><y_0.7969><class_Text>

<x_0.2715><y_0.7937>Horse is alfo ufed in the military language, to ex-
preis the cavalry; or the body of foldiers who ferve on
horfeback.<x_0.9932><y_0.8383><class_Text>

<x_0.2734><y_0.8352>The horfe includes horfe guards, horfe grenadiers,
and troopers. Dragoons are alfo frequently compre-
hended under this name, though they fight on foot :
of thefe there are now 18 regiments; belides three re-<x_0.9902><y_0.8953><class_Text>
